sections.heading: Putting my life in your hands
sections.text:
Lord, I am dependent on you for everything. I truly live only when your will is being done in me, not when I get my own way.

I have nothing in myself that gives me a claim on you. I cannot point to my goodness, my spiritual strength, my understanding of your plans, or even my grip on your promises as though any of it earns your help. I come with empty hands, resting only on your mercy and your good pleasure.

If your kindness brings me low and shows me how needy, sinful, and helpless I really am, then blessed be your name. Even that is mercy, because it teaches me to stop pretending and to depend on you.
theological_themes: Dependence on God’s will rather than self-rule
Grace as God’s free mercy, not earned worthiness
God’s humbling work as a form of mercy

scripture_references.connection: Jesus himself models perfect surrender to the Father’s will in the face of suffering. This grounds the prayer’s desire to live by God’s will rather than personal preference.
Paul describes God’s saving purpose as flowing from his gracious will and pleasure, not from human merit. That supports the prayer’s refusal to claim any worthiness before God.

sections.heading: Trusting you before I feel it
sections.text:
Father, when my needs push me into prayer, let me see that even this is part of your preparation for mercy. Do not let me despise the emptiness that makes me call on you.

Teach me to honor you by believing you before I feel comfort, closeness, or certainty. It would be wrong for me to make my feelings the foundation of my faith. Your word, your character, and your promises must carry more weight with me than my changing heart.
theological_themes: Faith grounded in God’s truth rather than inward feeling
Need and weakness as occasions for prayer
Trusting God’s promises before visible comfort comes

scripture_references.connection: Paul contrasts walking by faith with walking by sight. This directly supports trusting God’s revealed character and promises even when experience or emotion does not yet confirm them.
The passage teaches that coming to God requires faith in who he is and in his willingness to respond. It fits the prayer’s concern to believe God before receiving felt assurance.

sections.heading: Letting you search what is wrong in me
sections.text:
Please show me the sins that cloud my sight of you and make your love seem hidden from me. Do not let me protect what is separating me from fellowship with you.

Humble me for the evil I have already done. Give me a clear and settled desire to walk more carefully before you. I know that careless sin cannot give me assurance. If I live with no concern for holiness, how can I honestly take comfort that I belong to you?
theological_themes: Sin can damage experienced fellowship with God
Holy living as evidence of salvation, not the purchase of it

scripture_references.connection: The psalmist asks God to search and expose what is grievous within him, which matches this prayer’s request for God to reveal hidden sins and lead the heart back to him.
John connects fellowship with God to walking in the light, honest confession, and cleansing. This supports the prayer’s concern that cherished sin disrupts communion and calls for repentance.
Peter urges believers to confirm their calling and election through a life of growing godliness. This helps frame holiness as evidence that strengthens assurance, not as the basis of justification.

sections.heading: Learning the humility that receives grace
sections.text:
Make me meek and humble before you. Those are the people you teach, forgive, heal, and draw close to yourself. Let me rest by faith on your grace instead of arguing my own case.

Bring me to life where I am cold. Make me holy where I am still bent toward sin. Let my life give real evidence of your love at work in me, not so I can boast, but so I can know that your grace has not left me unchanged.
theological_themes: Humility as the posture of those taught by God
Sanctification as evidence of God’s love and saving work

scripture_references.connection: This passage speaks of the Lord instructing sinners, leading the humble, making his covenant known, and showing steadfast love. It closely reflects the prayer’s claim that the meek and humble are taught, pardoned, and brought into covenant fellowship.

Paul teaches that saving grace trains God’s people to turn from ungodliness and live devoted lives. This supports the prayer’s request that grace would not merely pardon but also sanctify and make obedience visible.

sections.heading: Praying until your will is done in me
sections.text:
Help me pray with faith so that I may come to know and embrace your will. Teach me to lean hard on your generous mercy and to believe that you will give what you have promised.

Strengthen me to pray knowing that anything I receive from you is a gift. Keep me asking, seeking, and waiting until you answer in the way that is right.

Grow my faith. I know it begins weak and incomplete. Open my heart wider and wider to you, like dry, cracked ground opening for rain. Let prayer stretch my trust and prepare me to receive whatever mercy you choose to give.

So I will wait for your will, ask for your will to be done, and by your grace become fully obedient to you.
theological_themes: Prayer as dependence on God’s promised mercy
Perseverance in prayer without demanding control

scripture_references.connection: John ties confidence in prayer to asking according to God’s will. This grounds the section’s desire to pray in faith while still submitting to God’s wisdom and purposes.
Jesus teaches his disciples to continue praying and not lose heart. That supports the prayer’s request for perseverance until God answers in his own way and time.

James encourages believers to ask God in faith for what they lack, especially wisdom, because God gives generously. This fits the prayer’s dependence on God’s free gifts and the need for growing faith.

content_provenance.original_author: Unattributed Puritan source (compiled and edited by Arthur Bennett)
content_provenance.original_source: The Valley of Vision: A Collection of Puritan Prayers and Devotions, ed. Arthur Bennett (The Banner of Truth Trust)
content_provenance.source_copyright_status: Compilation, titles and arrangement in copyright (Banner of Truth, 1975); underlying Puritan sources are public domain.
content_provenance.modern_version_note: Contemporary prayer based on the theological themes and ideas of the historical source; not a reproduction of the original wording.

theological_issues_identified: The original links holy walking with assurance of salvation. I preserved this as holiness being evidence that strengthens assurance, not as the ground of justification or a way to earn salvation.

The line about different degrees of mercy arising from different degrees of prayer could be misunderstood as a mechanical or transactional view of prayer. I rendered it as God using persevering prayer to grow faith and prepare the believer to receive mercy, while keeping God’s gifts free and governed by his will.

The original phrase about mercy making the speaker “poor and vile” is spiritually forceful and self-abasing. I interpreted it as God mercifully exposing need, sin, and helplessness rather than as a statement about material poverty being inherently blessed.
significant_interpretive_choices: I treated “I hang on thee” as total dependence on God rather than merely emotional attachment, because the rest of the prayer emphasizes God’s will, mercy, providence, and promises.
I rendered “believing before I feel” as trusting God’s word, character, and promises before receiving emotional comfort, to preserve the original’s warning against making feelings the basis of faith.
I interpreted “sins hide thee from me and eclipse thy love” as sins disrupting the believer’s experienced fellowship and assurance, not as God ceasing to love his child.
I kept the image of dry, cracked ground opening for rain because it concretely expresses weak faith widening in longing and readiness for God’s mercy.
